slides: Welcome back, and now the change graph. It's very rare on the exam. But it's hard and confusing, so it's good to know its trick before we meet it.
In a change graph, the values are not amounts. Each value is a change.

slides.say: This graph shows the volunteers in an organization called Green Light, over ten weeks. Each point is the change at the end of a week, compared with the end of the week before.
at: compared with the end of the week before

slides.say: Above zero, volunteers joined. Below zero, volunteers left.
The example says, at the end of the second week there were ten more volunteers than at the end of the first week.
And the point of week two is at plus ten. Ten more than the week before. It matches.
Let's say there were a hundred volunteers at the end of week one. Then at the end of week two there were a hundred ten.
Here's the confusing part. Look at week three. The line goes down into it. So it feels like volunteers left.
But the point of week three says plus five. Plus five means five more volunteers than the week before.
So it's a rise. A hundred ten plus five is a hundred fifteen.
That's why we ignore the line. We look only at the points.
Here's a sample question. In how many of the weeks was there no change in the number of volunteers?
at: In how many of the weeks

slides.say: What does no change mean? The change was zero. So we look for points at zero.
Let's take the line away, so it doesn't confuse us.
The points at zero are weeks five, nine and ten. That's three weeks.
Now let's bring the line back, to see how it fools us.
Into week five, the line falls. It looks like a drop. But the point of week five is zero, so nothing changed. Week five ended with the same number as week four.
Into week nine, the line rises. But the point is zero again. No change.

slides: So the answer is three weeks.

slides.say: One more question. At the end of week two there were seventy-five volunteers. How many were there at the end of week six?
at: At the end of week two

slides: We start from seventy-five, and we add the changes one week at a time. Only the points, no line.

slides.say: Week three is plus five. Seventy-five plus five is eighty.
Week four is plus five again. Eighty plus five is eighty-five.
Week five is zero. So it stays eighty-five.
Week six is minus ten. Eighty-five minus ten is seventy-five.
So at the end of week six there were seventy-five volunteers.

slides: This graph is confusing, so watch this video again if you need to. And remember the one rule. Ignore the line, and look only at the points.
That's the last type of chart. Next, we'll solve full chart sets. I'll see you in the next video.
